quizzes.stem: A response reports `cache_read_input_tokens` of 8,000, `cache_creation_input_tokens` of 0 and `input_tokens` of 40. How many input tokens did the request carry?

explanation.d: The page gives "total_input_tokens = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens", so 8,000 + 0 + 40.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the page sum adds a third term, and "total_input_tokens = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens" includes the 40.
explanation.c: Ruled out because that field holds only "tokens after the last breakpoint, which are not cached".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the sum "total_input_tokens = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens" has no subtraction.

quizzes.stem: A team marks a 1,500-token system prompt with `cache_control` on Claude Haiku 4.5 and sees both cache fields at 0, with no error. What explains it?

options.a: The text is under that model's 4,096 minimum, so it was handled as ordinary input
options.b: The text is over that model's minimum, so the API is quietly returning stored answers
options.c: The marker was ignored because system prompts are outside what the cache can hold
options.d: The five-minute lifetime had lapsed before the first request was even sent

explanation.a: The page says "Any requests to cache fewer than this number of tokens will be processed without caching" and gives 4,096 for Claude Haiku 4.5.
explanation.b: Ruled out because 1,500 is below the minimum, and "the prompt was not cached" is what two zeros mean.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page's hierarchy runs "up to and including the block designated with" the marker, and a system block can be that block.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Row 1 writes the 600 tokens" on a first request, so there is no earlier entry to lapse.

quizzes.stem: A request puts a block with the current clock reading ahead of a large stable policy, with the marker on the policy. Every call writes everything and never reads. Why?

options.a: The clock block counts as a second marker, which triggers a fresh write on each turn
options.b: The hash covers the marked block, so the policy is compared by itself and the clock is ignored
options.c: All content before the boundary feeds the hash, so a changing line gives a new one
options.d: The hash is rebuilt from the user question, which differs on each turn of the chat

explanation.c: The page says "The cache key is a hash of everything from the start of the request up to the marked block", so a changing block before it gives a new key.
explanation.b: Ruled out because that same sentence says the key is "a hash of everything from the start of the request", not of one block.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Cache breakpoints themselves don't add any cost." and only a block carrying `cache_control` is a breakpoint.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Row 2, a minute later, reads them and pays for only the new question".

quizzes.stem: A support bot reuses a 20,000-token prefix once every 40 minutes, around the clock. Which choice does the page's guidance favour?

options.a: The default TTL, since each reuse refreshes the entry free of charge and keeps it alive
options.b: The one-hour TTL, since the gap is past the default but within the hour
options.c: Neither TTL, since an entry survives through frequent use alone
options.d: Both TTLs together, since each request has to carry the pair of settings

explanation.b: The page recommends the one-hour TTL for prompts used "less frequently than 5 minutes, but more frequently than every hour".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the entry is "refreshed for no additional cost each time the cached content is used", and a 40-minute gap lets the default entry lapse first.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the one-hour TTL exists for "less frequently than 5 minutes, but more frequently than every hour".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "You can use both 1-hour and 5-minute cache controls in the same request" is allowed, not required.

quizzes.stem: A conversation adds 25 blocks between two requests, with one breakpoint on the final block. The second request misses the earlier write. What fixes it?

options.a: A label on the request, so the older entry is found by name
options.b: A longer TTL on the last marker, so the older entry survives until the next request
options.c: A larger `max_tokens`, so the search can reach further back through the blocks
options.d: A further marker near the older spot, so a fresh entry builds up there

explanation.d: The page says a second breakpoint near the older position starts a second lookback window there, since "You can define up to 4 cache breakpoints".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the miss comes from the window: "It checks at most 20 positions", and a longer TTL does not widen it.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the search "walks backward one block at a time", and `max_tokens` governs the reply.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the search is "looking for an entry an earlier request wrote", by hash, not by a label.

quizzes.stem: A team adds an image to the fifth message of a long conversation. Which parts of the cache are invalidated?

options.a: Only the tool list, while the instructions and the dialogue stay intact
options.b: Only the dialogue blocks; the tool list and instructions stay intact
options.c: The instructions and the dialogue, while the tool list stays intact
options.d: Nothing, since pictures sit outside the cached text

explanation.b: The page says "Adding/removing images anywhere in the prompt affects message blocks", and the table shows ✓ for tools and system.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels", and tools come first.
explanation.c: Ruled out because that pattern belongs to "Enabling/disabling web search modifies the system prompt", not to images.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Adding/removing images anywhere in the prompt affects message blocks".

quizzes.stem: A service fires ten calls together, all sharing a 30,000-token prefix, against a cold cache. What does the module predict?

options.a: One writes and nine read, since all ten share the same hash and the same prefix
options.b: Each one writes, as the entry appears only once a first reply starts
options.c: All read, since the entry is created the moment a request arrives
options.d: One writes and nine fail, since an entry allows a single writer

explanation.b: The page says a cache entry "only becomes available after the first response begins", so all ten write.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the entry "only becomes available after the first response begins", so the others have nothing to read.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the same sentence says it is available only "after the first response begins".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the advice is "wait for the first response before sending subsequent requests", not that extra requests fail.

quizzes.stem: A prefix is sent twice within five minutes on a model that reads at 0.1 times the base price. How does the spend on the pair compare with two ordinary sends?

options.d: About the same as two plain sends

explanation.a: A five-minute write at 1.25 plus a read at 0.1 gives 1.35 against 2, about two thirds.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the first send alone costs more than that: "5-minute cache write tokens are 1.25 times the base input tokens price".
explanation.c: Ruled out because that figure is the one-hour case, from "1-hour cache write tokens are 2 times the base input tokens price".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the second send is a read: "Cache read tokens are 0.1 times the base input tokens price".

quizzes.stem: A request marks the system block with a five-minute breakpoint and the final message with a one-hour breakpoint. What does the module say?

options.a: It violates the ordering rule, since the longer entry has to come first
options.b: It is accepted, with both entries billed at one common rate
options.c: It is accepted, with only the short entry written
options.d: It violates a one-TTL rule, since a request carries one lifetime

explanation.a: The page says "Cache entries with longer TTL must appear before shorter TTLs".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the writes are billed differently: "1-hour cache write tokens are 2 times the base input tokens price".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "The usage object then splits the writes" by lifetime, so both can be written.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "You can use both 1-hour and 5-minute cache controls in the same request" when ordered correctly.

quizzes.stem: A 600-token system prompt is marked on a model whose minimum is 512, and usage shows a write on every call and no reads. The prompt begins with the clock reading. What should the team do?

options.a: Pad the prompt so it clears the floor by a wider margin and stays well above it
options.b: Raise the TTL to an hour so the entry survives between uses and keeps being read
options.c: Shift that line to the end and set the boundary where unchanging text stops
options.d: Switch to a larger number of explicit markers so more segments are cached separately

explanation.c: The planner puts "a volatile block moves to the very end of the request", after the last breakpoint.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels", whatever the TTL.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the prompt already clears 512 tokens and usage shows writes, and the cause is "a volatile block moves to the very end" in the plan.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "You can define up to 4 cache breakpoints", yet an earlier changing block still changes the hash.
